title: Igneous Rocks
intro: Igneous rocks form when molten rock cools. Learn three things: HOW rock melts (pressure drops, volatiles added, heat added), WHY the melt differs (silica, partial melting, fractional crystallization), and HOW to name the rock (texture plus minerals on the classification chart).

sections.title: Magma, lava, intrusive, extrusive
bullets: The crust and the upper mantle (asthenosphere) are **mostly solid rock**. Melts only form in **localized areas** (small pockets), not everywhere.

boxes.text: Why is the hot deep Earth mostly solid? Pressure squeezes rock so hard that it needs MORE heat to melt (on a pressure-temperature graph the melting line, the solidus, slopes to the right). Only where pressure drops, volatiles are added, or extra heat arrives does rock cross that line and melt.
Magma is in the Mine (underground). Lava Lands on the surface. Ex-trusive = EXits the Earth; In-trusive = pushes IN to the rock.
Magma and lava are the SAME stuff. The name only depends on location, not on composition. 'Intrusive vs extrusive' is also about location (below vs above ground).

steps.title: The rock cycle
bullets: This is the **rock cycle**. Rock keeps changing from one type to another.
Igneous rock is what you get when molten rock (a **melt**) cools and turns solid.

img.alt: A photo of lava erupting at the surface next to a drawing of a magma chamber feeding a volcano.

steps.title: Lava versus magma
bullets: **Magma** = molten rock below the surface. **Lava** = molten rock at or above the surface.
Magma has three parts: the **melt** (liquid made of ions), solids (crystals floating in it) and **volatiles** (dissolved gases like water vapour, carbon dioxide, sulfur, chlorine).

img.alt: Cross-section of a volcano with the extrusive realm above ground and the intrusive realm, including the magma chamber, below ground.

steps.title: Above ground and below ground
bullets: **Intrusive** (also called plutonic) rock forms below ground, in the intrusive realm.
**Extrusive** (volcanic) rock forms above ground. Extrusive products are lava flow, ash cloud, ash fall, ash flow and volcanic debris flow.

sections.title: Three ways rock melts
bullets: There are **three causes of melting**: decompression, flux (volatiles) and heat transfer.

**Decompression melting** (pressure-relief melting): pressure (P) decreases but temperature (T) stays constant, so a melt forms. It happens at a mantle plume, a continental rift and a mid-ocean ridge. On the pressure-temperature graph (temperature across the top, pressure and depth down the side) the real temperature with depth is the geotherm. The **solidus** is where melting starts and the liquidus is where it is fully melted. Moving a rock from point A up to point B drops its pressure and carries it across the solidus. The geotherm of a normal stable plate never crosses the solidus, so no magma forms there.

boxes.text: Why does flux melting work with no change in pressure or temperature? Volatiles lower the melting point of the rock. It is like salt on an icy road: the ice melts even though the weather did not warm up.
Why does falling pressure cause melting? High pressure holds the minerals tight in a solid. A rock that rises keeps its heat but loses the pressure, so it now sits beyond its (lower) melting point.
Pick the cause by asking what changed: Pressure drops = decompression. Volatiles added = flux. Heat added = heat transfer. (P, V, H)

Decompression melting does NOT need the rock to get hotter. Flux melting does NOT need the rock to get hotter either. Only heat transfer adds heat. Textbook adds that a hotspot is decompression plus extra heat, but the slide lists the mantle plume under decompression.

steps.title: Flux melting: add volatiles
bullets: **Flux melting**: volatiles help break chemical bonds, creating a melt.
No extra heat and no pressure drop is needed. The volatiles do the work.

img.alt: Labelled drawing of flux melting at a subduction zone: volatiles leave the sinking plate and the asthenosphere above it melts to feed a volcanic arc.

steps.title: Flux melting at a subduction zone
bullets: The sinking slab releases volatiles into the asthenosphere above it.
That asthenosphere melts, and the melt feeds the **volcanic arc**.

img.alt: Drawing of heat-transfer melting: hot magma pools at the base of the crust and heat rising from it melts the crust above.

steps.title: Heat-transfer melting
bullets: **Heat from magma melts adjacent rocks.** Hot magma pools at the base of the crust and the heat rising from it melts the crust itself.
A volcano over melted crust erupts cooler melt (yellow). A volcano over deeper magma erupts hotter melt (red).
Heat-induced melting is the least common way to make magma.

sections.title: Melting by tectonic setting
bullets: **Hot spots** are **intraplate** (inside a plate) sites of active plutonism (magma cooling underground) and volcanism. Hawaii is the example.

A massive **plume** of anomalously hot mantle rock sits under active hot spots and rises slowly because it is **buoyant** (lighter) compared with the rock around it. Plumes can be newly forming, mature or extinct, and some form at shallow locations (about 600 km). The Hawaii plume reaches down toward the core-mantle boundary. Hotspot chains form as a plate moves over a stationary plume (the Hawaii-Emperor chain).

boxes.text: Why do plumes rise? A plume is hotter, so it is less dense than the surrounding mantle. Lower density means it floats upward, like a hot air balloon.
Where is the volcano? Ridge, rift and hotspot = rising rock (decompression). Subduction = sinking slab with water (flux).

Hot spots are NOT at plate boundaries; they are intraplate (inside a plate). Also: transform faults have shallow earthquakes but almost no volcanism, so 'flux melting at a transform fault' is wrong (practice midterm Q2 and Q23).

steps.title: Subduction zones
bullets: At a **subduction zone** one plate sinks. A trench and a **volcanic arc** form (for example the Aleutian arc).
The melting type here is **flux melting**.
Arc magma evolves to silica-rich rock such as andesite and rhyolite.

img.alt: World map with an inset of a mid-ocean ridge and drawings of pillow basalts forming under water.

steps.title: Mid-ocean ridges and rifts
bullets: At a **mid-ocean ridge** the melting type is **decompression melting**. Ocean-floor volcanoes are basaltic because partial melting of ultramafic mantle makes basalt.
Lava erupting under water makes **pillow basalts**: older pillows pile up and a new pillow forms.
A **continental rift** (the East African Rift on the map) is similar: plates pull apart, the crust thins, and rock rises and decompresses.

img.alt: Drawing of a mantle plume head and fissure eruptions, a map of the Columbia River flood basalts, and a photo of layered basalt cliffs.

steps.title: Large igneous provinces
bullets: **Large Igneous Provinces (LIPs)** are huge areas of **flood basalts** over mantle hot spots. Fissure eruptions pour out the basalt, as in the Columbia River flood basalts.
Examples: Siberian, Deccan, Columbia, Parana, Karoo, Kerguelen, Ontong Java, Iceland, Caribbean.
The Deccan Traps cover about a third of India. The Siberian Traps may be linked to the biggest mass extinction.

sections.title: Melt types: silica, density, viscosity
bullets: Take-home: the silica content of a melt sets its viscosity and, in the end, the name of the melt.

boxes.text: Why is felsic lava thick? Silica links into long tangled chains. More silica plus cooler temperature means stickier. Thick magma also traps gas, so pressure builds and it blasts out explosively.
FELsic = FELdspar + silica, light colour, thick like toothpaste. MAFic = MAgnesium + Fe (iron), dark, runny.

Slide ranges: felsic 66-76, intermediate 52-66, mafic 45-52, ultramafic 38-45. The textbook gives different round numbers (felsic 65-75, intermediate 55-60, mafic 45-50, ultramafic 40 or less). Use the slide's numbers.

sourceNotes: Silica chains idea in the first why box is outside source

steps.title: Four melt types by silica
bullets: Melts are sorted into four types by **% silica (SiO2)**: felsic 66 to 76%, intermediate 52 to 66%, mafic 45 to 52%, ultramafic 38 to 45%.
The arrow shows silica increases toward felsic. Example rocks: rhyolite (felsic), diorite (intermediate), gabbro (mafic).

img.alt: Table comparing density, temperature, silica and viscosity of felsic, intermediate, mafic and ultramafic melts, with photos of felsic, intermediate and mafic rocks.

steps.title: Four melt types compared
bullets: Felsic: very low density, very low temperature (**600 to 850 C**), **very high viscosity**, explosive eruptions. Intermediate: low density, low temperature, high viscosity, explosive.
Mafic: high density, high temperature, **low viscosity**, thin hot runny eruptions. Ultramafic: very high density, very high temperature (up to **1,300 C**), very low viscosity.

img.alt: Bullet list on viscosity with drawings of runny lava flows and a lava fountain above and a thick lava dome below.

steps.title: Viscosity and melt movement
bullets: **Viscosity** = resistance to flow (syrup is runny, toothpaste is thick). It depends on **temperature, volatile content and % silica**.
Low viscosity = hotter, less SiO2 (mafic), typically fewer volatiles. Think lava flows and a lava fountain.
High viscosity = cooler, more SiO2 (felsic), typically more volatiles. Think of a lava dome.

sections.title: Why do melts vary?
bullets: Partial melting of crust by heat from magma gives magma that is **more felsic** than the original rock. This is how silica-rich granitic continents grew.

boxes.text: Why does partial melting raise silica? Think of a chocolate chip cookie warmed gently: the easy-to-melt parts go first. In rock the easy-to-melt minerals are the silica-rich ones, so the first liquid is richer in silica than the leftover solid.
Partial melting = only part of it melts. Assimilation = the magma assimilates (swallows) the wall rock.
Partial melting does not copy the source. Ultramafic mantle does not make ultramafic magma; it makes mafic magma (practice midterm Q24).

images.alt: Table of the four categories of magma by weight percent silica.
Graph of silica content of magma against rising temperature with circles showing rock going from no melt to partial melt to nearly complete melt.
Drawing of a magma body with wall rock melting into it and blocks of rock falling in and dissolving.

img.alt: Table of the four categories of magma by weight percent silica.

steps.title: The source rock matters
bullets: The **source rock** sets the first melt composition in many cases.
The table lists the four melt types by silica again: felsic 66 to 76%, intermediate 52 to 66%, mafic 45 to 52%, ultramafic 38 to 45%.

img.alt: Graph of silica content of magma against rising temperature with circles showing rock going from no melt to partial melt to nearly complete melt.

steps.title: Partial melting
bullets: Rock is a mixture of minerals and they melt at different temperatures, so only part of it melts. This is **partial melting**.
The graph shows magma is rich in silica at low temperature (little melt) and its silica share falls as temperature rises. The circles go from no melt, to partial melt, to nearly complete melt.

The low-melting, silica-rich parts melt first. Partial melting of ultramafic mantle (peridotite) makes **mafic (basaltic) magma**, which has MORE silica than its source. Magma is also less dense than rock, so it rises.

img.alt: Drawing of a magma body with wall rock melting into it and blocks of rock falling in and dissolving.

steps.title: Assimilation
bullets: **Assimilation**: partial melting of wall rock makes new magma that mixes with magma from below. Blocks of rock also fall into the magma and dissolve.
**Xenoliths** are unmelted pieces of country rock inside igneous rock.
When mafic magma rises slowly through thick felsic continental crust, it assimilates felsic rock and can arrive as intermediate or felsic magma.

sections.title: Fractional crystallization and Bowen's series
bullets: Crystal fractionation works best in continents, where a longer trip to the surface gives more time.

boxes.text: Why does the leftover liquid get more silica-rich? The early crystals (olivine, pyroxene) take Mg and Fe out of the liquid and sink to the bottom. What is left has less Mg and Fe, so the share of silica goes up.
Bowen's series is a ladder with the same order as ultramafic to felsic. First to crystallize = last to melt. Olivine is at the top and quartz at the bottom.

Temperatures differ by source. The slide scale runs about 1400 down to 800; the textbook says about 1,250 down to about 700 C. The order of minerals is what matters. Also: fractional crystallization (crystals leave, melt becomes felsic) is the opposite of partial melting (midterm example Q5).

head: Series
Minerals, first to last (high T to low T)
rows: K-feldspar, muscovite, quartz (last to crystallize, first to melt)

steps.title: Mafic crystals leave first
bullets: Mafic minerals crystallize first; felsic minerals crystallize last. This is **fractional crystallization**.
The original melt is mafic. As it cools, mafic crystals form and settle out. After they settle, the remaining magma becomes **more felsic**.

img.alt: Drawing of a cooling mafic melt where olivine and Ca-rich plagioclase form first, then pyroxene and Na-rich plagioclase, leaving a leftover melt that makes felsic rock.

steps.title: Which minerals form when
bullets: A mafic melt starts to cool. **Olivine and Ca-rich plagioclase** form first and settle out.
Later **pyroxene and Na-rich plagioclase** form.
If the leftover (residual) melt escapes and freezes, it makes felsic rock.

img.alt: Bowen's reaction series chart with the discontinuous and continuous branches, temperature scale and rock types from ultramafic to felsic.

steps.title: Bowen's reaction series
bullets: Two branches. **Discontinuous series**: olivine, pyroxene, amphibole, biotite. **Continuous series**: plagioclase, from Ca-rich to Na-rich. Both finish with K-feldspar, muscovite and quartz.

Top = first to crystallize (last to melt), high temperature (1400 on the scale). Bottom = last to crystallize (first to melt), low temperature (800). The right edge lists ultramafic, mafic, intermediate, felsic from top to bottom, so the type of melt can be read off the series.

Toward felsic there is more silica, sodium, aluminum and potassium; the other way there is more iron, magnesium and calcium. Mafic rocks form at higher temperatures than felsic ones, and felsic lavas erupt hundreds of degrees cooler.

sections.title: The classification chart (texture + composition)
bullets: Igneous rocks are classified by **texture** (grain size, cooling history) and **composition** (felsic, intermediate, mafic, ultramafic).

Granite is a good match for continental crust. Basalt makes up the ocean floor and is the most common rock on Earth's surface. Gabbro is a major part of the lower oceanic crust. Komatiite is rare and mostly Archean. The classes have no sharp borders in nature.

boxes.text: Why does a fine grain mean fast cooling? Crystals need time to grow. Lava on the surface loses heat quickly into air and water, so many tiny crystals form (or glass). Magma deep underground sits in warm rock and cools slowly, so crystals grow large.

Chart code: Fine = Fast = Flows (volcanic). Coarse = slow = deep. Pairs: rhyolite with granite (felsic), andesite with diorite, basalt with gabbro. Fine name first, coarse name second, same composition.

The mineral bars are approximate, not exact. A rock that matches a bar roughly is that rock (midterm example Q6, Q7 and practice Q21 are answered this way). Texture alone does not tell composition, and composition alone does not tell texture.

images.alt: Cross-section of a volcano and magma body showing small drops and thin flows cooling quickly, a large blob cooling slowly and a shallow sheet cooling faster than a deep sheet.
Diagram comparing a small and a large ball of melt, and a flat pancake shape and a sphere, to show which cools faster.
Classification chart for crystalline igneous rocks with fine and coarse rock names, side arrows for temperature, density and silica, and mineral percentage bars.

img.alt: Cross-section of a volcano and magma body showing small drops and thin flows cooling quickly, a large blob cooling slowly and a shallow sheet cooling faster than a deep sheet.

steps.title: Cooling near the surface or deep
bullets: Small drops and thin flows cool quickly. A large blob cools slowly.
A shallow sheet cools faster than a deep sheet, because the wall rock is cooler near the surface and warmer deeper.

img.alt: Diagram comparing a small and a large ball of melt, and a flat pancake shape and a sphere, to show which cools faster.

steps.title: Size and shape change cooling
bullets: For the same shape, a **smaller volume** cools faster.
For the same volume, a **pancake shape** (more surface area) cools faster than a sphere.

img.alt: Classification chart for crystalline igneous rocks with fine and coarse rock names, side arrows for temperature, density and silica, and mineral percentage bars.

steps.title: The classification chart
bullets: How to use it: (1) look at grain size, fine (cooled fast, extrusive, aphanitic) or coarse (cooled slowly, intrusive, phaneritic); (2) look at the minerals and their percentages on the bars; (3) find the row whose bar matches; (4) read the rock name in the fine or coarse column.
Moving from felsic down to ultramafic, **freezing temperature rises** (about 600 to 1,250 C), density rises (about 2.5 to 3.4 g/cm3) and silica falls (about 70% to 40%).
Mineral key: Q quartz, K K-feldspar, B biotite, P plagioclase, A amphibole, Px pyroxene, O olivine. The percentages in the table below are read by eye from the bars (about 3% either way).

sections.title: Textures and fragmental rocks
bullets: **Vesicular**: gas bubbles trapped in lava leave holes called **vesicles**. Scoria is a vesicular rock. Pumice is a froth of glass so full of vesicles that it can float.

boxes.text: Why do volatiles make bubbles? Magma holds gas dissolved under pressure. When it rises, pressure drops and the gas comes out of solution, like fizz in a soda bottle when you open it. If the lava freezes right then, the bubbles are locked in.
PHAneritic = PHysically visible crystals. APHanitic = cannot see them. Porphyritic = big crystals floating in a fine, pasty groundmass.

Glass is not a mineral (no crystal structure), so obsidian is not a mineral (practice midterm Q12). Slide 42 groups pumice and scoria with glassy rocks, while the textbook calls scoria vesicular and pumice glassy froth. Fastest cooling texture is glassy; slowest is pegmatitic.

What you see
Cooling story

steps.title: Three basic textures
bullets: **Crystalline texture**: interlocking crystals. **Fragmental texture**: broken pieces, seen under a microscope.
**Glassy texture**: no crystals at all, because lava cooled so fast that none formed. Glassy rocks include pumice, scoria and obsidian (volcanic glass that breaks with a curved, conchoidal fracture).

img.alt: Two rock samples side by side, a fine-grained aphanitic rock and a coarse-grained phaneritic rock with visible crystals.

steps.title: Crystal size: fine to giant
bullets: **Aphanitic** = grains too small to see, fast cooling, extrusive. **Phaneritic** = crystals you can see, slow cooling, intrusive.
**Porphyritic**: big crystals (**phenocrysts**) sitting in a fine groundmass. This means two-stage cooling: slowly at depth first, then quickly nearer the surface.
**Pegmatitic**: extremely large crystals from very slow crystallization of leftover fluid.

img.alt: Photos of a layered ash deposit with a group of people for scale, an ash cloud over a pyroclastic flow, and a golf ball-sized fragment.

steps.title: Pyroclastic rocks
bullets: **Pyroclastic rocks** are made of **tephra** thrown out of explosive eruptions. Examples: tuff and volcanic breccia. Welded tuff forms when hot fragments stick together.
The pictures show a layered ash deposit, an ash cloud above a pyroclastic flow, and a golf ball-sized fragment.
Fragment sizes: ash under 2 mm, lapilli 2 to 64 mm, bombs or blocks over 64 mm.

sections.title: Dikes and sills
bullets: **Dikes run vertically, while sills run horizontally.** Both are **tabular intrusions** (flat, sheet-like).
A dike is **discordant** (cuts across layers). A sill is **concordant** (runs parallel to the layers). Both are younger than the rock around them, which helps geologists date rock sequences.

boxes.text: Why does magma make a sill or a dike? Magma looks for the weakest path. Sideways between layers is weak (sill). A vertical crack is also weak (dike).
SILL = lies flat, like a window sill. DIKE = stands up and cuts across, like a wall.
Younger vs older: a dike or sill is YOUNGER than the layers it cuts or lies between. Do not say it is the same age as the surrounding rock.

images.alt: Two block drawings of a sill: magma squeezes between rock layers and lifts the layers above it.
A photo of Antarctic mountains with a geologist's sketch labelling a sill between sandstone and coal-rich beds.
Photo of Shiprock, New Mexico, with thin dike walls radiating from the eroded volcanic neck.

img.alt: Two block drawings of a sill: magma squeezes between rock layers and lifts the layers above it.

steps.title: How a sill forms
bullets: Magma squeezes **between** layers and lifts the layers above it. The arrow shows the roof being pushed up.

img.alt: A photo of Antarctic mountains with a geologist's sketch labelling a sill between sandstone and coal-rich beds.

steps.title: A real sill
bullets: A sill in the Antarctic mountains. The 'What a Geologist Sees' sketch shows it as a flat band lying between layers.

img.alt: Photo of Shiprock, New Mexico, with thin dike walls radiating from the eroded volcanic neck.

steps.title: Dikes and Shiprock
bullets: Magma fills cracks that cut across the layers, so the rock is pushed sideways.
Dikes cut at a high angle across pre-existing layering (bedding or foliation). They can occur in **swarms**, like the three dikes radiating from **Shiprock, New Mexico**, an eroded volcanic neck.

sections.title: Plutons, batholiths and exposing them
bullets: A **pluton** is a body of intrusive rock: a mass of magma that cooled underground. Its heat **bakes the wall rock**, leaving a baked zone along the contact between the granite and the wall rock. Chunks of wall rock can end up inside the granite as xenoliths.
A **stock** is a smaller intrusive body than a batholith. Most landforms made by igneous rocks are intrusive bodies, because big crystals are tougher and last longer than extrusive rock.

boxes.text: Why do we see plutons at the surface at all? They formed deep underground. Over millions of years erosion removes the rock on top and exposes them.
Batholith = the BIG one (many plutons joined) under big mountain ranges, such as the Sierra Nevada.
Slides show batholiths as granite (felsic). Do not confuse a batholith (big, discordant, felsic) with a laccolith (small blister, concordant, between layers).

steps.title: Exposing igneous features, Time 1
bullets: At Time 1 the picture shows volcanoes, a lava flow, a laccolith and magma chambers.
A **laccolith** is a blister-like concordant intrusion between layers. A downward-bulging one is a **lopolith**.
At Time 3, after **erosion** strips the top, the plutons stand out as hills.

steps.title: Exposing igneous features, Time 2
bullets: At Time 2 the picture shows a dike, a lava plateau, a sill and a pluton.
A pluton pushes up its roof, stretching and folding the crust, faulting it and sending dikes upward.

img.alt: Photo of jagged granite peaks of the Bugaboos with a climber in the foreground.

steps.title: Batholiths and granite peaks
bullets: A **batholith** is many plutons merged, more than 100 km2, linked to subduction zones and mostly felsic.
Exposed batholiths in western North America include the Coast Ranges, Idaho, Sierra Nevada and Peninsular. The granite of Yosemite (Half Dome) belongs to the Sierra Nevada batholith.
The Bugaboos are granite peaks.

sections.title: Volcano types
bullets: Volcano shape follows the viscosity idea: runny magma builds broad low cones, sticky magma builds steep ones.
**Shield volcano**: broad, low-angle flanks, mafic, low viscosity, gentle **effusive** eruptions (Kilauea, Mauna Loa). Found at hotspots, ridges, rifts.
**Stratovolcano** (composite): steep, symmetrical cone, felsic to intermediate, viscous, **explosive** (Rainier, Fuji). Typical of subduction zones.
**Lava dome**: very thick felsic lava piles up at the vent. **Caldera**: a basin left when the roof collapses into an emptied magma chamber (Crater Lake, Yellowstone).
**Cinder cone**: small, steep, mafic with lots of volatiles (Paricutin, 1943). **Flood basalts**: giant, very low viscosity basalt eruptions.
Most dangerous hazard: **pyroclastic flows**, hot mixtures of gas, ash and blocks. Others: ash fall, landslides, lahars (volcanic mudflows), toxic gases.

boxes.text: Why do shield volcanoes have low slopes? Their runny basalt spreads far before freezing. Why are stratovolcanoes steep? Sticky lava piles up near the vent.
Shield = runny and wide (like a warrior's shield lying on the ground). Strato = layers of ash and lava, steep and dangerous.
Hawaii vs Mount St. Helens: St. Helens magma has MORE silica and gas, so it is more viscous and explosive. It is not hotter (felsic magma is cooler).

sourceNotes: Volcano types are not covered in the slides; textbook only

sections.title: Practice questions: composition and melting
bullets: Which does NOT describe a composition? ultramafic, felsic, intermediate, mafic, **porphyritic** (porphyritic is a texture). Answer: **E**.
Which of these is a texture, not a composition? basaltic, **aphanitic**, dioritic, rhyolitic, peridotitic. Aphanitic is the texture; the others name compositions. Answer: **B**.
Which element is not associated with felsic? Si, Na, K, **Ca**, Al. Si, Na, Al and K go with felsic; Fe, Mg and Ca go with the mafic side. Answer: **D (Ca)**.
Pressure relief melting is what results in hot rock melting when it convects upwards. Answer: **D**.

What would you argue to show that this is not a valid argument: 'today's subduction zones make few felsic rocks, so fluxing is not the cause'? Answer: **B** (mantle convection used to be faster, so volumes of volatiles in subduction zones were greater).

boxes.text: Texture words (aphanitic, phaneritic, porphyritic, glassy) describe grain size. Composition words (felsic, mafic, basaltic, granitic and so on) describe chemistry and minerals. The exam likes asking which word is the odd one out.
Ask yourself: is this word about HOW BIG the crystals are (texture) or WHAT it is made of (composition)?
'Porphyritic' and 'aphanitic' end in -itic like 'dioritic' and 'peridotitic'. Check what the word describes, not how it sounds.

quiz.q: A volcano erupts. The same molten rock that sat in a chamber underground is now flowing down the outside of the cone. What is the correct name for the molten rock in each place?
options: Lava underground, magma at the surface
Magma underground, lava at the surface
Tephra underground, magma at the surface
quiz.why: Magma is molten rock below the surface; lava is molten rock at or above it. Same material, new name when it reaches the surface.

quiz.q: Which statement about intrusive and extrusive igneous rocks is INCORRECT?
options: Extrusive rocks usually cool more slowly than intrusive rocks
Intrusive rocks form below ground from magma
Extrusive rocks form at or above the surface from lava
Intrusive rocks usually have large crystals
Extrusive rocks usually have small crystals or glass
quiz.why: Surface lava loses heat fast, so extrusive rocks cool faster (fine grains). Intrusive rocks cool slowly underground and grow big crystals.

quiz.q: A rock rising in a mantle plume stays at about the same temperature but starts to melt near the top. Why?
options: Friction with the lithosphere heats it up
Water is added from a sinking slab
The rock gets cooler as it rises, which makes it melt
Lower pressure lowers its melting point, so it crosses the solidus
quiz.why: This is decompression melting: pressure drops, T stays constant, and the rock now sits beyond its melting line.

quiz.q:
Consider these statements about flux melting:
I. Volatiles help break chemical bonds, making a melt.
II. It occurs above a subducting slab that releases water.
III. It happens when pressure drops and temperature stays constant.
Which are correct?
quiz.why: I and II describe flux melting. III describes decompression melting.

quiz.q: Which pairing of a tectonic setting with its magma-producing process is INCORRECT?
options: Subduction zone: flux melting from added water
Continental crust above a basalt intrusion: heat-transfer melting
Transform fault: flux melting from added water
quiz.why: Flux melting needs a subducting slab releasing water. Transform faults have shallow earthquakes and almost no volcanism.

quiz.q:
Which of the following produces magmas?
(a) pressure relief melting
(b) felsic crystallization
(c) fluxing by volatiles
(d) all of the above
(e) both (a) and (c)
quiz.why: Pressure relief (decompression) and fluxing both create melt. Crystallization turns melt into solid, so it does not produce magma.

quiz.q:
Consider these statements about hot spots:
I. Mantle plumes rise because they are buoyant compared with the surrounding rock.
II. Large igneous provinces of flood basalts form above mantle hot spots.
III. Hot spots occur only at plate boundaries.
Which are correct?
quiz.why: I and II are true: plumes are buoyant and flood basalts form above hot spots. Hot spots are intraplate sites, so III is false.

quiz.q: A magma contains 48% SiO2 by weight. Based on the silica table, what type is it and how does it behave?
options: Felsic, very high viscosity, explosive eruptions
Mafic, low viscosity, thin and runny when it erupts
Impossible to say from the table
quiz.why: 45 to 52% SiO2 is mafic: low viscosity, thin hot runny eruptions.

quiz.q: Which statement about viscosity is NOT correct?
options: Magma with more SiO2 flows more easily than magma with less SiO2
Cooler magma is more viscous than hotter magma
Felsic magma typically contains more volatiles than mafic magma
Viscosity depends on temperature, volatile content and silica content
quiz.why: More silica means HIGHER viscosity (thicker). So felsic flows less easily than mafic.

quiz.q:
Mount St. Helens erupts explosively while Hawaiian volcanoes erupt gentle lava flows. Which factor best explains the difference?
(a) Hawaiian magma has more silica
(b) St. Helens magma has more silica and gas, so it is more viscous and traps gas until it blasts out
(c) St. Helens magma is hotter
(d) Hawaiian volcanoes are on a subduction zone
(e) Both (a) and (c)
options: (b) St. Helens magma has more silica and gas, so it is more viscous and traps gas until it blasts out
(d) Hawaiian volcanoes are on a subduction zone
quiz.why: Felsic to intermediate magma is cooler, high in silica and gas, and very viscous. Hawaiian mafic magma is runny, so gas escapes.

quiz.q: Which of the following elements is NOT associated with felsic composition?
quiz.why: Silica, sodium, aluminum and potassium increase toward felsic; iron, magnesium and calcium go with the mafic side.

quiz.q: Which of the following does NOT describe a rock composition?
quiz.why: Phaneritic is a texture (visible crystals). The others are compositions.

quiz.q: Partial melting of the ultramafic mantle (peridotite) produces a magma that is:
options: Ultramafic, exactly the same as its source
Mafic (basaltic), richer in silica than its source
Lower in silica than its source
quiz.why: The silica-rich minerals melt first, so the melt has more silica than the source. Mantle peridotite gives basalt.

quiz.q: A mafic magma slowly rises through thick felsic continental crust and arrives at the surface as intermediate or felsic magma. What process best explains this?
options: Heating by a mantle plume only
quiz.why: Pieces of felsic wall rock melt into or dissolve in the magma, which adds silica.

quiz.q: What is the opposite of fractional crystallization?
quiz.why: Fractional crystallization removes the first crystals from a cooling melt. Partial melting makes a melt from only part of a rock.

quiz.q: In a basaltic magma chamber, early-formed olivine and pyroxene crystals sink to the bottom. How does the remaining liquid change?
options: It becomes richer in Mg and Fe
quiz.why: Olivine and pyroxene take Mg and Fe out of the liquid, so the leftover magma becomes more silica-rich (more felsic).

quiz.q: Which of the following is one of the last minerals to crystallize during fractional crystallization?
quiz.why: Bowen's series ends with K-feldspar, muscovite and quartz at the bottom (lowest temperature). Olivine is first.

quiz.q:
Consider these statements about Bowen's reaction series:
I. Olivine and Ca-rich plagioclase crystallize early.
II. Quartz crystallizes late, at low temperature.
III. Felsic rocks crystallize at higher temperatures than mafic rocks.
Which are correct?
quiz.why: Mafic minerals crystallize at high temperature and felsic ones at low temperature. III is backwards.

quiz.q: Use the classification chart to pick rock names for this rock: K-feldspar 25%; quartz 37%; plagioclase 33%; biotite 5%.
options: that rock composition is not included in the figure
quiz.why: The felsic bar is about 40% quartz, 32% plagioclase, 18% K-feldspar and a few % biotite. This mix is close to it, so the rock is rhyolite (fine) or granite (coarse).

quiz.q: Use the classification chart to pick rock names for this rock: olivine 85%; pyroxene 15%.
options: that rock composition is not included in the figure
quiz.why: The ultramafic bar is about 83% olivine and 17% pyroxene, so this is ultramafic: komatiite (fine) or peridotite (coarse).

quiz.q: Using the igneous classification chart: a FINE-grained rock is about 60% plagioclase, 25% amphibole, 10% biotite and under 5% quartz. What is it?
options: That composition is not in the figure
quiz.why: The intermediate bar is mostly plagioclase (~61%) with amphibole (~27%). Fine grained makes it andesite, not diorite (coarse).

quiz.q: An igneous rock has large, well-formed crystals sitting in a fine-grained groundmass. What does this tell you about its cooling history?
options: It cooled the whole time quickly
It cooled the whole time slowly
It cooled quickly first, then slowly
It cooled slowly at depth first, then quickly at or near the surface
quiz.why: Porphyritic texture means a two-stage history: big phenocrysts grew slowly, then the rest froze fast.

quiz.q: Which igneous texture indicates the FASTEST cooling?
quiz.why: Glassy rock (obsidian) cooled so fast that no crystals formed at all.

quiz.q: Two lava bodies have the same volume. One is a thin flat sheet; the other is a round blob. Which cools faster, and what texture would it likely show?
options: The thin sheet, because more surface area means faster cooling; likely finer grains
The blob, because it holds more heat; likely finer grains
Both cool at the same rate
The thin sheet, but it will have larger crystals
The blob, and it will be glassy
quiz.why: For the same volume, a pancake shape has more surface area and cools faster. Faster cooling gives smaller crystals.

quiz.q: Which statement about dikes and sills is INCORRECT?
options: A dike runs vertically and cuts across layers
A sill cuts vertically across layers and a dike runs horizontally between them
A sill runs horizontally between layers
Both are younger than the rock they intrude
quiz.why: It is the other way round: dikes are vertical and cut across layers; sills are horizontal and run parallel to layers.

cards.back: Magma is molten rock below Earth's surface. Lava is molten rock at or above the surface.
Intrusive rock forms below ground (slow cooling, large crystals). Extrusive rock forms above ground (fast cooling, small crystals or glass).
Decompression (pressure drops), flux melting (volatiles added), and heat transfer (heat from magma).
Pressure decreases while temperature stays constant, so the rock crosses its melting point and a melt forms.
Mantle plumes (hot spots), continental rifts and mid-ocean ridges.
Volatiles help break chemical bonds and lower the melting point, creating a melt. Happens above subducting slabs.
Heat from magma melts adjacent rocks, such as the crust above a magma body.
The line on a pressure-temperature graph where melting starts. Solid to the left, melt to the right.
How fast temperature rises with depth: about 25 C per km in the upper 100 km.
Flux melting: the sinking slab releases volatiles into the overlying asthenosphere, which melts.
Decompression melting as rising mantle loses pressure; mid-ocean ridges make basalt and pillow basalts.
An intraplate site of active plutonism and volcanism over a buoyant mantle plume.
A huge area of flood basalts that forms above mantle hot spots, for example Siberian, Deccan, Columbia River.
Felsic 66-76%, intermediate 52-66%, mafic 45-52%, ultramafic 38-45% SiO2.
66-76% SiO2, very low density, very low temperature (600-850 C), very high viscosity, explosive eruptions.
45-52% SiO2, high density, high temperature, low viscosity: thin, hot, runny eruptions.
38-45% SiO2, very high density, up to 1,300 C, very low viscosity.
Temperature, volatile content and % silica. Cooler, more silica and more volatiles means higher viscosity.
Only some minerals melt (the lower melting point, silica-rich ones first), so the melt differs from the source rock.
Partial melting of ultramafic peridotite makes mafic (basaltic) magma, richer in silica than the source.
Wall rock melts into, or blocks fall into and dissolve in, the magma, changing its composition (often more felsic).
An unmelted piece of country rock inside an igneous rock.
cards.short: Foreign rock chunk in igneous rock

cards.back: Mafic minerals crystallize first and settle out; the remaining magma becomes more felsic.
cards.short: Early crystals leave, melt turns felsic

cards.back: Partial melting.
Discontinuous: olivine, pyroxene, amphibole, biotite. Continuous: Ca to Na plagioclase. Then K-feldspar, muscovite, quartz.
First: olivine and Ca-rich plagioclase (high temperature, last to melt). Last: quartz (low temperature, first to melt).
Grains too small to see; fast cooling; extrusive (example: rhyolite, basalt).
Crystals large enough to see; slow cooling; intrusive (example: granite, gabbro).
Large phenocrysts in a fine groundmass; slow cooling at depth, then fast cooling nearer the surface.
Very large crystals from very slow crystallization of leftover fluid.
Holes (vesicles) left by trapped gas bubbles; scoria is a common example.
No crystals because of extremely fast cooling; obsidian. It is the fastest-cooling texture.
Pumice: froth of glass full of vesicles, can float. Scoria: vesicular volcanic rock.
Made of tephra thrown out in explosive eruptions: tuff, welded tuff, volcanic breccia. Ash under 2 mm, lapilli 2-64 mm, bombs over 64 mm.
Felsic: rhyolite (fine), granite (coarse). Intermediate: andesite, diorite. Mafic: basalt, gabbro. Ultramafic: komatiite, peridotite.
Smaller volume cools faster. A flat pancake shape cools faster than a sphere. A shallow sheet cools faster than a deep one.
A dike cuts across layers (vertical). A sill runs along layers (horizontal). Both are younger than the rock around them.
Many plutons merged, over 100 km2, mostly felsic granite, found in the cores of mountain ranges such as the Sierra Nevada.
